title: Amazon Raises Minimum Pay to $20 an Hour, Adds Whole Foods Discounts
excerpt: The $1.5 billion pay raise lifts starting wages for US full-time fulfillment and delivery workers to $20 an hour starting September 27, with average pay near $24 — plus new Whole Foods grocery discounts and a lifetime no-fee banking benefit.
body:
• Amazon is raising minimum starting pay for US full-time core operations workers to $20 an hour, with average pay reaching nearly $24 and average total compensation above $32 including benefits.
  • The $1-an-hour raise represents a $1.5 billion investment; the new pay rate takes effect September 27.
  • New benefits include an uncapped 10% grocery discount online and 20% off in-store at Whole Foods, plus "Day 1 Financial" — a lifetime First Tech Federal Credit Union membership with zero overdraft fees.
  • The move arrives just before the holiday season, when Amazon historically hires around 250,000 seasonal workers.

Amazon is raising the minimum starting pay for its US full-time core operations employees — fulfillment center workers and delivery drivers — to $20 an hour, alongside a new grocery discount and a lifetime banking benefit aimed at making "everyday life more affordable" for its workforce.

The $1-per-hour increase, announced Wednesday in a blog post by Udit Madan, senior vice president of Worldwide Operations, brings average hourly pay across Amazon's US core operations workforce to nearly $24. "When you add in the value of our industry-leading benefits, average total compensation comes to more than $32 per hour," Madan wrote. The company is investing more than $1.5 billion in the raises — about 0.06% of its $2.68 trillion market capitalization, as TechCrunch noted.

The new pay rate takes effect September 27. Amazon says its minimum starting pay has risen more than 17% over the past three years.

What's in the package

The announcement pairs the raise with three new benefits. The headline grabber is groceries: an uncapped 10% discount on eligible fresh groceries and everyday essentials ordered through Amazon.com and Whole Foods Market online, plus 20% off in-store at Whole Foods Market, the premium chain Amazon owns. The discount can be combined with existing Prime member discounts, and will be available to every US Amazon employee starting October 1.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=i2qywJVYFBc

Worker reaction was mixed. On a subreddit for Amazon fulfillment center employees, one worker quipped about the Whole Foods discount: "So it would make it cost almost the same as a regular store, then?" — a reference to the chain's historically higher prices.

The second benefit is financial: "Day 1 Financial," a membership in First Tech Federal Credit Union offering qualified employees and their families low-cost banking services they can keep for life. The accounts carry $0 overdraft fees and no account minimums on standard checking and savings, plus access to credit cards and loans. No credit history is required to open checking and savings accounts — a meaningful detail for workers new to the US financial system. Rollout begins later this year and becomes broadly available in 2027.

These join an existing benefits stack that includes free Prime memberships, healthcare starting at $5 a week with $5 copays, and prepaid education programs.

The labor-market context

Amazon's move lands in a labor market where warehouse wages have been climbing and rivals are competing for the same workers. Walmart, Amazon's closest competitor for hourly labor, expanded its 10% employee discount last year to cover nearly all grocery purchases; its starting pay is $14 an hour, with US hourly employees averaging more than $18.50. For Walmart's warehouse and supply-network workers, average hourly pay is $27.50 — ahead of Amazon's new average, though Walmart's footprint is smaller.

The timing is also seasonal. Amazon is gearing up for the holidays, when it sees a massive surge in orders; last year it hired an estimated 250,000 seasonal workers — about half of all seasonal retail hiring in the US. Higher starting pay and grocery perks sharpen its pitch to seasonal hires who may convert to permanent roles.

Fast Company pointed out the broader backdrop: by the end of 2026, the minimum wage will have crossed $15 in 14 states and 65 cities and counties, according to the National Employment Law Project, with many jurisdictions at $17 or higher. In Seattle, Amazon's hometown, the minimum wage already exceeds $21 — above the company's new national floor.

"When you add in the value of our industry-leading benefits, average total compensation comes to more than $32 per hour."

— Udit Madan, Senior Vice President, Worldwide Operations, Amazon

Why it matters for immigrant workers

Amazon's core operations workforce is heavily immigrant — warehouse and delivery roles are among the largest employers of newcomers to the United States, including many from the Indian diaspora. For these workers, the no-credit-history banking benefit may matter as much as the dollar-an-hour raise: establishing a US financial footprint is one of the earliest hurdles for recent arrivals.

The announcement also carries a diaspora footnote of its own: it was authored by Udit Madan, the Indian-origin executive who runs Amazon's global operations, one of the most senior Indians in corporate America.

What to watch next

The pay raise takes effect September 27, with grocery discounts following October 1 and the banking rollout phasing in through 2027. Whether competitors match the package — and whether the perks translate into lower turnover in Amazon's notoriously high-churn warehouses — will determine whether Wednesday's announcement was a genuine reset in frontline retail compensation or a well-timed holiday hiring campaign.
